_comment: One-line explanations for the short videos, one per question. Each was written against the official question and answer. German inside a line is marked [[like this]] so the narrator pronounces it in German. Questions 72, 73 and 75 ask who holds an office now: their lines explain the office and tell viewers to check the current answer.
1: Criticising the government is protected by [[Meinungsfreiheit]], freedom of expression. In a democracy, open debate is allowed and nobody may be punished just for their opinion.
2: Religious education is the one school subject named in the Basic Law. Parents decide about it until age 14, and from then on young people choose for themselves.
3: In a [[Rechtsstaat]], the law is above everyone. Residents, officials and the government itself must all follow it, and courts can check that they do.
4: Freedom of expression is one of the basic rights, the [[Grundrechte]], in the first articles of the Basic Law. They protect each person against the power of the state.
5: A free vote means nobody may pressure or force you, and your choice brings you no disadvantage. That is also why voting in Germany happens in secret.
6: Germany's constitution is the [[Grundgesetz]], the Basic Law of 1949. It was meant as a temporary text until reunification, and it stayed after 1990.
7: Freedom of faith and conscience means people may believe in any religion or none at all, and live by their conscience. The state may not force a belief on anyone.
8: The Basic Law promises equal rights and equal treatment, not equal wealth. Germany's economy lets income differ while social support protects people in need.
9: Asylum protects people persecuted in their home country, so it is meant for foreigners. The Basic Law says it plainly: [[Politisch Verfolgte genießen Asylrecht]].
10: A fine is a lawful punishment decided by a court. Harsher penalties are another matter: Article 102 of the Basic Law states that the death penalty is abolished.
11: The [[Grundgesetz]] was written in 1949 for West Germany as a provisional framework. Since reunification in 1990, it has been the constitution of the whole country.
12: Press freedom is a basic right, and no single party can take it away. The Basic Law also says the core of a basic right may never be touched.
13: The opposition is every member of parliament outside the governing parties. They question and criticise the government, which keeps its power in check.
14: Freedom of expression covers every medium, from a conversation to a post online. The same limits apply everywhere, such as laws against insults and incitement.
15: The Basic Law forbids forced labour, [[Zwangsarbeit]]. People are free to choose their own work, a clear answer to the forced labour of the Nazi era.
16: Free speech ends where it harms the honour of others. Spreading false claims about a person in public can be punished, because their reputation is protected too.
17: Article 3 of the Basic Law says all people are equal before the law. The state may not favour or disadvantage anyone because of their origin, faith or gender.
18: Article 1 opens the Basic Law with [[Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar]]: human dignity is inviolable. Every part of the state must respect and protect it.
19: Freedom of movement, [[Freizügigkeit]], means people may decide for themselves where in Germany they live. No authority assigns a town or region to them.
20: A dictatorship would destroy democracy, so the aim is [[verfassungswidrig]], unconstitutional. Germany can even ban such a party to defend its free order.
21: The federal coat of arms shows the [[Bundesadler]], a black eagle with red beak and claws on a gold shield. You see it on passports and in the Bundestag.
22: Germany is a republic: no king or queen inherits power. Even the head of state, the Federal President, is elected and serves a fixed term of five years.
23: Most working people in Germany are employees. They work for a company or a public authority, rather than running their own business as self-employed people.
24: Germany has 16 [[Bundesländer]], or federal states. Three of them are cities on their own: Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen.
25: Alsace-Lorraine, [[Elsass-Lothringen]], belongs to France. It was part of the German Empire from 1871 to 1918, but it is not one of today's 16 states.
26: Article 20 of the Basic Law calls Germany a democratic and social federal state. Power comes from the people, the state supports those in need, and the states share power.
27: Germany is a [[Bundesstaat]], a federal state. Power is shared between the federal level and the 16 states, which each have their own parliament and government.
28: Members of the [[Bundestag]] are chosen by the eligible voters in a general election. German citizens can vote in these elections from the age of 18.
29: An eagle, the [[Bundesadler]], is on the federal coat of arms. The eagle has been a symbol of power in German lands for many centuries.
30: Press censorship has no place in a democracy. The Basic Law says it in four words: [[Eine Zensur findet nicht statt]], there is no censorship.
31: One party rarely wins a majority alone, so several parties form a [[Koalition]]. They set out their shared plans in a coalition agreement before governing together.
32: Germany has three state powers: making laws, governing, and judging. The press is independent and is not one of them.
33: Germany has no state church. The state stays neutral towards all faiths, so people are free to follow any religion or none, and religious groups run their own affairs.
34: Germany is not a monarchy. The emperor gave up the throne in 1918, and today every position of state power is filled by election or appointment, never by birth.
35: Social security is paid for mainly by [[Sozialabgaben]], contributions taken from wages. Employees and employers usually share the cost between them.
36: Health insurance, [[Krankenversicherung]], is a pillar of social security. Introduced under Bismarck in 1883, it helps pay for doctors and hospital care.
37: Most states are led by a [[Ministerpräsident]] or [[Ministerpräsidentin]]. The city-states differ: Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen are led by a mayor.
38: The Basic Law calls Germany a democratic and social [[Bundesstaat]]. Federal means the country is built from 16 states that share power with the federal level.
39: Every federal state has its own government and its own parliament, the [[Landtag]]. That is why rules on things like schools and police can differ between states.
40: The anthem begins [[Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit]], unity and justice and freedom. Only this third verse of the old song is sung as the anthem today.
41: Citizens hold many different views, and parties give those views a voice. Competing parties also give voters a real choice and let governments change peacefully.
42: New federal laws are passed by parliament, mainly the [[Bundestag]]. The [[Bundesrat]], which represents the states, also takes part in the process.
43: Only the [[Bundesverfassungsgericht]], the Federal Constitutional Court, can ban a party, and only if it fights the free democratic order. The bar is set very high.
44: Citizens cannot vote directly for the Federal President. A special body, the [[Bundesversammlung]], elects the head of state every five years.
45: Long-term care insurance, [[Pflegeversicherung]], is part of social insurance. It is the youngest branch, next to health, pension, unemployment and accident insurance.
46: Building roads and schools is a public task paid for with taxes. Federal, state and local governments share these jobs, so everyone can use them.
47: The state does not pay for anyone's holiday travel. Tax money goes to shared needs such as roads, schools, the police and support for people in need.
48: There is no national citizens' assembly among the constitutional bodies. Those include the [[Bundestag]], the [[Bundesrat]], the federal government and the Federal President.
49: Schools are the business of the states, the [[Bundesländer]]. That is why school types and holiday dates can differ depending on where you live.
50: Germany's system is the [[soziale Marktwirtschaft]], the social market economy. Companies compete freely, while the state protects workers and supports people in need.
51: In a state under the rule of law, only the official police may arrest someone, and only with a legal reason. A judge must then decide quickly on any detention.
52: Article 20 of the Basic Law says [[Alle Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus]]: all state authority comes from the people, who exercise it in elections and votes.
53: A [[Rechtsstaat]] binds the state itself to the law. If an authority makes a decision someone thinks is unlawful, they can challenge it in court.
54: State power is split into three branches: making laws, carrying them out, and judging. A directive is a type of instruction, not a branch of government.
55: This is the [[Reichstag]] building in Berlin, the seat of the [[Bundestag]] since 1999. Visitors can climb its glass dome and look down into the debating chamber.
56: The [[Ordnungsamt]], the public order office, belongs to the town or city administration. It deals with local matters such as parking checks and noise complaints.
57: By tradition, the largest parliamentary group, or [[Fraktion]], proposes the President of the Bundestag. This person chairs the sessions and keeps order in debates.
58: The Chancellor chooses the ministers, but the Federal President formally appoints them. The same happens when a minister is dismissed, on the Chancellor's proposal.
59: Jewish life in Germany goes back about 1,700 years. A Roman decree from the year 321 already mentions a Jewish community in Cologne.
60: Both chambers take part in making federal laws, so they belong to the legislative branch. The word comes from the Latin lex, which means law.
61: In a democracy, all power comes from the people. The [[Grundgesetz]] says it directly: [[Alle Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus]].
62: Each of the sixteen states has its own parliament, usually called the [[Landtag]], and voters choose it in a [[Landtagswahl]].
63: Police, tax offices and ministries carry out the law, so they are executive. The courts judge independently and form their own branch, the judiciary.
64: Germany works on three levels: the federation, the sixteen states, and the local municipalities. In German that is [[Bund, Länder und Kommunen]].
65: The Bundestag makes laws, controls the government and elects the chancellor. The cabinet is formed by the chancellor, who proposes the ministers.
66: Berlin and Munich, two of the biggest cities in Germany, are home to the largest Jewish communities in the country today.
67: Schools are mainly the business of the sixteen states. That is why school systems, and even school holidays, differ from one state to the next.
68: The [[Grundgesetz]] places the whole school system under the supervision of the state. So the state oversees education because the constitution says so.
69: Below the federation and the states come the municipalities, or [[Gemeinden]]. They handle local matters close to people's daily lives.
70: The Federal President proposes a candidate for chancellor, and the [[Bundestag]] then votes. Running the government is the chancellor's job.
71: Since the government moved from Bonn, both the chancellor's office, the [[Bundeskanzleramt]], and the [[Bundestag]] are in Berlin.
72: The [[Bundeskanzler]] leads the federal government and sets its direction. This answer changes with each new government, so check it again close to your test.
73: Parliamentary groups, [[Fraktionen]], are the parties' teams in the [[Bundestag]]. Their size changes with every election, so check this one before your test.
74: The [[Bundestag]] is the national parliament, elected by the people. It meets in the historic [[Reichstag]] building in Berlin.
75: The Federal President is the head of state, elected for five years by the [[Bundesversammlung]]. The answer changes after each election, so check it before your test.
76: CDU means [[Christlich Demokratische Union]]. This center-right party has produced chancellors such as Konrad Adenauer, Helmut Kohl and Angela Merkel.
77: The [[Bundeswehr]] is Germany's military. It is called a parliamentary army, because the [[Bundestag]] must approve armed missions abroad.
78: SPD stands for [[Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands]]. It is the oldest party still active in Germany, with roots in the workers' movement.
79: FDP means [[Freie Demokratische Partei]], a liberal party that focuses on individual freedom and a market economy.
80: The Federal Constitutional Court, the [[Bundesverfassungsgericht]] in Karlsruhe, interprets the Basic Law and can strike down laws that violate it.
81: The people elect the [[Bundestag]], and the [[Bundestag]] elects the chancellor. So voters choose the head of government indirectly.
82: The Federal Chancellor heads the cabinet and sets the main guidelines of government policy, which the ministers then follow in their own areas.
83: Germans do not vote for the chancellor directly. The Federal President proposes a candidate, and the members of the [[Bundestag]] elect them.
84: The Federal President is the head of state and represents Germany at home and abroad. Day-to-day governing is left to the chancellor and the cabinet.
85: The [[Bundesrat]] is made up of members of the sixteen state governments. Through it, the states have a say in federal laws.
86: The [[Bundesversammlung]] meets only to elect the president. It has all members of the [[Bundestag]] plus an equal number of delegates from the states.
87: The Federal President is the head of state. The chancellor leads the government, but the president represents the country as a whole.
88: The opposition is made up of the parties not in government. They question, criticize and control the government and offer alternatives.
89: Members of parliament from the same party work together as a group called a [[Fraktion]]. Groups get speaking time and seats on committees.
90: Through the [[Bundesrat]], the state governments take part in federal lawmaking. Many laws need its approval before they can pass.
91: State governments send members to the [[Bundesrat]]. If a state election shifts the majority there, the federal government may struggle to pass laws.
92: CSU stands for [[Christlich-Soziale Union]]. It runs only in Bavaria and is the sister party of the CDU, which does not run there.
93: The second vote, or [[Zweitstimme]], is a vote for a party. It decides how many seats each party gets in the [[Bundestag]].
94: To vote in a federal election, you must be at least 18. Some states let 16-year-olds vote in local or state elections, but not for the [[Bundestag]].
95: Children in Germany must go to school. This is called [[Schulpflicht]], and home schooling is generally not allowed in its place.
96: Denying the Holocaust is a crime in Germany. It can be punished with up to five years in prison or a fine, to protect the dignity of the victims.
97: With a regular job, contributions to [[Sozialversicherung]] are taken straight from your pay. They fund health care, pensions and unemployment insurance.
98: A government needs a majority in the [[Bundestag]]. If members switch to another group, the numbers can change and the majority can be lost.
99: Social insurance is shared: employers and employees each pay a part of the contributions. This sharing is a basic idea of the German welfare state.
100: Pension, unemployment and long-term care insurance are part of the statutory system. Life insurance is a private contract that people choose themselves.
101: Trade unions, or [[Gewerkschaften]], represent employees. They negotiate with employers about wages and working conditions.
102: The [[Bundesverdienstkreuz]] is Germany's order of merit. The Federal President awards it to people for outstanding service to society.
103: The name comes from the party colors: red for the SPD, yellow for the FDP, and green for the Greens, like a traffic light, or [[Ampel]].
104: Pregnancy is strongly protected at work. Under [[Mutterschutz]] rules, an employer generally may not dismiss someone because they are expecting a child.
105: Election workers, or [[Wahlhelfer]], run the polling stations and count the votes once voting ends. The count is public, so anyone may watch.
106: Volunteers staff the polling stations on election day. When the polls close, they count the ballots, and the counting is open to the public.
107: The [[Bundestag]] is elected for four years. This period is called a [[Wahlperiode]], and after it the voters decide again.
108: Federal elections are for German citizens who are at least 18. Living in Germany alone is not enough to vote for the [[Bundestag]].
109: Federal elections normally take place every four years, because each [[Bundestag]] is elected for a four-year term.
110: A term of the [[Bundestag]] lasts four years. An early election is possible only in special cases, such as a failed vote of confidence.
111: Criticizing Israeli policy is free speech in Germany. Publicly calling for the destruction of Israel, however, is prohibited.
112: German elections are secret: nobody may see how you vote. The [[Grundgesetz]] also requires them to be general, direct, free and equal.
113: The party with the most votes wins the election. Seats in parliament are shared out roughly in proportion to the votes each party receives.
114: Voting is a right, not a duty. There is no compulsory voting in Germany, so each citizen decides freely whether to vote.
115: Active suffrage, [[aktives Wahlrecht]], is the right to vote. Passive suffrage, [[passives Wahlrecht]], is the right to stand for election.
116: The right to cast a vote is called [[aktives Wahlrecht]]. The right to be elected yourself is called [[passives Wahlrecht]].
117: Parties need at least five percent of second votes to enter the [[Bundestag]]. This [[Fünf-Prozent-Hürde]] keeps parliament from splitting into many tiny parties.
118: The [[Makkabi]] clubs grew out of Jewish tradition, but membership is open to all. Anyone can join, whatever their religion or origin, in the spirit of sport.
119: Free elections mean nobody may pressure you. You decide yourself whether to vote at all and whom to choose, and in Germany voting is a right, not a duty.
120: With the [[Erststimme]] you choose a local candidate by majority, and the [[Zweitstimme]] decides each party's share of seats. Germany combines both methods.
121: As a rule, a party needs at least five percent of the second votes to enter the [[Bundestag]]. Germans call this the [[Fünfprozenthürde]], the five percent hurdle.
122: Free, equal and secret: no one forces your choice, every vote counts the same, and nobody may see how you voted. The [[Grundgesetz]] adds general and direct.
123: The five percent hurdle is the minimum share of votes a party needs to win seats in parliament. It keeps very small parties out and the parliament workable.
124: In the [[Bundestagswahl]], voters elect the national parliament. The chancellor is not elected directly; the members of parliament choose the chancellor afterwards.
125: Regular elections let voters replace a government peacefully. If most voters want a change, power passes to others without force or revolution.
126: Before an election, the municipality sends each eligible voter a [[Wahlbenachrichtigung]]. It shows the polling station and can be used to request a postal vote.
127: Many small parties in parliament make it hard to build a stable majority. The Weimar Republic suffered from exactly that, so the hurdle keeps the [[Bundestag]] workable.
128: People elected to parliament are members of parliament, in German [[Abgeordnete]]. They represent all citizens and are bound only by their conscience.
129: Of these, only the [[Bundestag]] is elected directly by the people. The chancellor is chosen by the [[Bundestag]], and the president by the [[Bundesversammlung]].
130: A valid ballot shows the choice clearly, with at most one cross in each of the two columns and no names, notes or extra marks that could identify the voter.
131: A mayor is the head of a [[Gemeinde]], a town or municipality, and leads its local administration. In most of Germany, residents elect their mayor directly.
132: Voluntary work, or [[Ehrenamt]], means helping without pay, for example in sports clubs, volunteer fire brigades or charities. Millions of people in Germany do it.
133: Postal voting, called [[Briefwahl]], lets you vote by mail before election day. Voting by phone or for someone else is not allowed, because every vote is personal.
134: A [[Bürgerinitiative]] is a group of residents who join forces on a local issue. Collecting signatures and talking to the council is a legitimate way to be heard.
135: Trade unions, or [[Gewerkschaften]], represent employees. They negotiate wages and working conditions with employers, often in collective agreements.
136: The [[Arbeitsgericht]] handles disputes between employees and employers, such as a dismissal a worker thinks is unfair. Rent and neighbor problems go elsewhere.
137: Workplace conflicts go to the labor court, the [[Arbeitsgericht]]. Germany has specialized courts for areas such as labor, social and administrative law.
138: After an unfair dismissal, you can file a [[Kündigungsschutzklage]] at the labor court. Act quickly: the deadline is three weeks after receiving the notice.
139: A criminal trial happens when the prosecution charges someone with a crime. Religion or opinion can never be the reason, since the [[Grundgesetz]] protects both.
140: Lay judges, called [[Schöffen]], are ordinary citizens who sit with professional judges. Together they decide whether someone is guilty and what the sentence is.
141: A lawyer, in German [[Rechtsanwältin]] or [[Rechtsanwalt]], advises people on legal questions and represents them in court. Judges decide; lawyers speak for one side.
142: Judges work at a court and deliver judgments, [[Urteile]] in German. They are independent and bound only by the law, not by orders from the government.
143: Judges belong to the judiciary, the [[Judikative]]. It is the branch that applies the law in courts, separate from parliament and the government.
144: Judges hold judicial power, the [[rechtsprechende Gewalt]]. It checks the other two powers, so courts can even review whether actions of the state are lawful.
145: Germany splits state power into three branches, known as [[Gewaltenteilung]]. Judges work for the judiciary, which decides cases independently.
146: A court proceeding is a trial, in German a [[Prozess]]. Most court hearings in Germany are public, so anyone can watch how justice is done.
147: Judges decide cases by applying the law. In German that is [[Recht sprechen]], literally to speak the law.
148: The police make sure laws are followed and protect public safety. Defending the country is a different job, done by the armed forces, the [[Bundeswehr]].
149: Denying the Holocaust is antisemitic because it rejects the murder of six million Jews. In Germany it is a crime, while fair criticism of a government is not.
150: A lay judge is an honorary judge, in German [[ehrenamtliche Richterin]] or [[ehrenamtlicher Richter]]. They need no law degree and serve alongside professional judges.
151: The GDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop its own people from fleeing to the West. Germans simply call it [[die Mauer]], and it fell in 1989.
152: The National Socialists ruled from 1933, when Hitler became chancellor, until 1945, when Germany was defeated at the end of the Second World War.
153: On May 8, 1945, the German armed forces surrendered unconditionally, ending the war in Europe. Germany remembers it as a day of liberation from National Socialism.
154: The Second World War ended in 1945, in Europe on May 8 and in Asia a few months later. Germany was then occupied and divided into four zones.
155: National Socialist rule lasted twelve years, from 1933 to 1945. It began when Hitler was appointed chancellor and ended with Germany's defeat in the war.
156: Hitler was appointed [[Reichskanzler]] on January 30, 1933. Within months the Nazis had dismantled democracy and set up a dictatorship.
157: In 1933 the Nazis set up a dictatorship: they banned other parties, ended free elections and persecuted opponents. All power lay with Hitler.
158: The so-called Third Reich was the Nazi dictatorship of 1933 to 1945. It had no free elections, no free press and no independent courts.
159: Under National Socialism there were no free elections. Censorship, arbitrary arrests and the persecution of Jews were all part of the dictatorship.
160: The Second World War began on September 1, 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and ended in 1945. It was the deadliest war in history.
161: The Nazi state was built on state racism. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped Jews of their rights, and this led on to persecution and genocide.
162: Stauffenberg, an army officer, placed a bomb in Hitler's headquarters on July 20, 1944. Hitler survived, but the attempt is remembered as a symbol of resistance.
163: In November 1938 the Nazis attacked synagogues and Jewish shops across Germany. These [[Novemberpogrome]] showed the persecution of Jews in the open.
164: On November 9, 1938, Nazis and their supporters burned synagogues and wrecked Jewish shops. Germany remembers it as the [[Reichspogromnacht]].
165: Konrad Adenauer became the first [[Bundeskanzler]] in 1949 and served until 1963. He tied West Germany firmly to the West and to European cooperation.
166: In 1989, people in the GDR marched every Monday, chanting [[Wir sind das Volk]], we are the people. These peaceful protests helped bring down the regime.
167: After 1945 Germany was occupied by four victors: the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France. Each ran its own zone, and Berlin was split the same way.
168: Japan was not an occupying power in Germany. It fought on Germany's side in the war, while the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France occupied the country.
169: The Federal Republic was founded in 1949, when the [[Grundgesetz]] came into force on May 23. The GDR followed in the east that October.
170: Under National Socialism, political parties were banned and only the Nazi party was allowed. Press freedom and human dignity were not protected.
171: In a [[soziale Marktwirtschaft]], supply and demand set prices, but the state adds protection such as health insurance and unemployment benefits.
172: The GDR was founded in 1949 in the Soviet occupation zone in the east. The three western zones became the Federal Republic the same year.
173: West Germany was one of six founding members of the European Economic Community in 1957, which grew into today's EU. It joined NATO and the UN only later.
174: The GDR was founded on October 7, 1949, a few months after the Federal Republic. Germany then stayed divided into two states until 1990.
175: Germany was split into four occupation zones, one each for the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France. Berlin was divided into four sectors too.
176: Britain took the north-west, the Soviet Union the east, the USA most of the south, and France the south-west, next to its own border.
177: Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, yet the four Allies split the city too: the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union each ran one sector.
178: When the Soviet Union cut every road, railway and canal into West Berlin, the Western Allies flew in food and coal instead. Berliners call it the [[Luftbrücke]], the air bridge.
179: Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945, which meant no conditions and no negotiations. The Allies then took over all authority in the country.
180: Konrad Adenauer became the first [[Bundeskanzler]] in 1949 and led West Germany for fourteen years, tying the young democracy firmly to the West.
181: In Warsaw, Willy Brandt knelt in silence at the memorial to the ghetto uprising. The gesture, known as the [[Kniefall von Warschau]], asked forgiveness for German crimes.
182: Jewish communities gather to pray and study in a synagogue, in German a [[Synagoge]]. A church serves Christians, and a mosque serves Muslims.
183: In the 1950s West Germany rebuilt fast after the war, with rising wages and booming exports. This period is called the [[Wirtschaftswunder]], the economic miracle.
184: In 1947 the United Nations General Assembly voted for a plan to partition Palestine, and Israel declared its independence on that basis in 1948.
185: The Iron Curtain was the heavily guarded border that cut Europe in two, sealing off the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact countries from the West during the Cold War.
186: On June 17, 1953, workers across the GDR rose up until Soviet tanks crushed the protest. West Germany kept the date as its Day of German Unity until 1990.
187: The GDR added a hammer, a compass and a wreath of grain to the black-red-gold flag. Together they stood for workers, intellectuals and farmers.
188: The wall went up on August 13, 1961, to stop the steady stream of people fleeing from East to West. It then divided the city for twenty-eight years.
189: So many people were leaving for the West that in 1961 the GDR sealed off West Berlin almost overnight. In German the wall is simply called [[die Mauer]].
190: GDR is short for German Democratic Republic, in German [[Deutsche Demokratische Republik]], or [[DDR]]. Despite the name, it was a one-party state.
191: After weeks of peaceful protests, the GDR opened its border on the night of November 9, 1989, and crowds streamed through the wall in Berlin.
192: Brandenburg is one of the five eastern states that once belonged to the GDR. It completely surrounds Berlin, and its capital is Potsdam.
193: From 1961 to 1989 a guarded wall separated East Berlin from West Berlin, cutting through streets and families. A long stretch survives as the East Side Gallery.
194: October 3 is the [[Tag der Deutschen Einheit]], the Day of German Unity. On that date in 1990, East and West Germany became one country again.
195: Saxony-Anhalt, in German [[Sachsen-Anhalt]], is one of the five eastern states that were part of the GDR. Its capital is Magdeburg, on the river Elbe.
196: [[Die Wende]] means the turning point. In autumn 1989 peaceful protests brought down the one-party state, leading to the first free elections in the GDR in 1990.
197: Thuringia, in German [[Thüringen]], was part of the GDR and joined the Federal Republic in 1990. Its capital is Erfurt, and it is often called the green heart of Germany.
198: Saxony, or [[Sachsen]], was part of the GDR and is one of the five eastern states today. Its capital is Dresden, and Leipzig became famous for the protests of 1989.
199: [[Stasi]] is short for [[Staatssicherheit]], state security. The ministry spied on its own citizens, and today people can ask to read the files kept about them.
200: [[Mecklenburg-Vorpommern]], on the Baltic coast, was part of the GDR. Its capital is Schwerin, and its largest city is the port of Rostock.
201: The five eastern states are Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. A list with any western state is wrong.
202: In the Cold War the GDR stood firmly in the Soviet-led Eastern bloc as a member of the Warsaw Pact. West Germany sat on the other side, in NATO.
203: In the GDR the state decided what was produced, how much, and at what price. That is a [[Planwirtschaft]], the opposite of a market economy.
204: The two states did not merge as equals. The five re-created eastern states joined the Federal Republic, and its [[Grundgesetz]] then applied to all of Germany.
205: West Germany was already a founding member of the European Community, today's EU. When the eastern states joined Germany, they joined it too, with no separate entry.
206: [[Stolpersteine]] are small brass plaques set into the pavement outside the last chosen homes of people persecuted by the Nazis, each one engraved with a name.
207: The GDR belonged to the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance led by the Soviet Union. West Germany was on the opposite side, having joined NATO in 1955.
208: The [[Stasi]] was the GDR's secret police and intelligence service. It watched its own population closely, using a huge network of unofficial informers.
209: The GDR's emblem showed a hammer and a compass inside a wreath of rye, standing for workers, intellectuals and farmers. The Federal Republic uses an eagle.
210: On June 17, 1953, strikes against higher work quotas spread into an uprising across the GDR. Soviet tanks ended it, but the day was never forgotten.
211: As Chancellor, Willy Brandt signed treaties with Moscow, Warsaw and Prague as part of his [[Ostpolitik]]. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971.
212: The official name is [[Bundesrepublik Deutschland]]. The word federal shows that the country is made up of sixteen states, the [[Länder]].
213: About 84 million people live in Germany, which makes it the most populous country in the European Union by a clear margin.
214: Black, red and gold, [[Schwarz-Rot-Gold]], come from the movement for unity and freedom in the 1800s. The [[Grundgesetz]] names them as the federal colors.
215: Helmut Kohl was Chancellor when the wall fell and steered the country to reunification in 1990. He served for sixteen years, from 1982 to 1998.
216: A large eagle, the [[Bundesadler]], hangs in the plenary chamber of the [[Bundestag]]. Because of its round shape, people nicknamed it the [[fette Henne]], the fat hen.
217: The GDR was founded in October 1949, a few months after the Federal Republic, and it ended when it joined the Federal Republic on October 3, 1990.
218: Five eastern states joined in 1990: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. That brought Germany to sixteen states.
219: Germany's borders were settled for good with reunification in 1990. The Two Plus Four Treaty confirmed them, including the border with Poland.
220: On January 27, 1945, Soviet troops liberated the Auschwitz camp. Germany now uses this date to remember all the victims of National Socialism.
221: Schengen removed routine checks at the borders between member countries, so people can usually cross without showing a passport. It is still wise to carry an ID card.
222: Switzerland borders Germany to the south, along Lake Constance and the Rhine. It is not in the EU, but it is part of the Schengen area.
223: Poland is Germany's neighbor to the east. For much of its length, the border follows the rivers Oder and Neisse, which were fixed as the frontier after 1945.
224: EU stands for European Union, in German [[Europäische Union]]. Germany was one of the six countries that started European cooperation in the 1950s.
225: German is the official language of Austria, in German [[Österreich]]. It is also widely spoken in Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Luxembourg.
226: Twelve gold stars in a circle on blue. The twelve stands for unity and completeness, not for the number of countries.
227: Denmark is Germany's only neighbor to the north, bordering the state of Schleswig-Holstein. A Danish minority lives on the German side of the border.
228: The GDR's accession in 1990 is called the [[Wiedervereinigung]], reunification, because Germany had been one country before it was divided after 1945.
229: Luxembourg borders Germany to the west, next to Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland. It is one of the six founding countries of today's European Union.
230: The European Parliament is elected every five years, around the same days in all member countries. Citizens of other EU countries living in Germany may vote here too.
231: European integration means countries growing closer step by step, sharing a single market, common rules and, for many, the euro. Six countries began it in the 1950s.
232: In the European elections, citizens vote directly for the members of the European Parliament. Germany elects more of them than any other member country.
233: The Czech Republic, in German [[Tschechien]], borders Germany to the east, along Bavaria and Saxony. Its capital is Prague.
234: The European Parliament's official seat is Strasbourg, in German [[Straßburg]], a French city near the German border. It also works in Brussels and Luxembourg.
235: Verdun saw terrible fighting between France and Germany in the First World War. Kohl and Mitterrand holding hands there in 1984 showed that old enemies now keep the peace.
236: The European Union has 27 member states. The number dropped from 28 when the United Kingdom left the EU in 2020.
237: Signed in 1957, the [[Römischen Verträge]] founded the European Economic Community, a common market that later grew into today's European Union.
238: The European Parliament holds its plenary sessions in Strasbourg, does committee work in Brussels, and has its administration in Luxembourg.
239: In 1957, West Germany signed the Treaties of Rome with France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, founding the EEC as one of six members.
240: Euro coins and notes arrived on 1 January 2002 and replaced the [[Deutsche Mark]]. The euro already existed for banking from 1999.
241: [[Elterngeld]] is not paid automatically. Parents apply at the [[Elterngeldstelle]], and it is paid back for at most three months before the application.
242: Kindergarten in Germany is voluntary, so the parents or legal guardians decide. They are the [[Erziehungsberechtigten]], those entitled to raise the child.
243: Outdoor demonstrations need no permission in Germany, but they must be registered, [[angemeldet]], in advance so the authorities can plan for safety.
244: The [[Abitur]] is the final exam at a [[Gymnasium]] and opens the way to university. Its official name is the [[allgemeine Hochschulreife]].
245: Sexual contact with a child under 14 is a crime in Germany, even if the child agrees. Since Anne is only 13, this relationship is not allowed.
246: At 18, people in Germany become legally adult, [[volljährig]]. They can sign contracts on their own and vote in federal elections.
247: This is [[Mutterschutz]]. It usually covers six weeks before the birth and eight weeks after, and it includes strong protection against dismissal.
248: The [[Grundgesetz]] calls raising children the natural right of parents and their first duty. The state only watches over how they carry it out.
249: Raising children is first the job of the parents, [[die Eltern]]. The state steps in only to support them or to protect a child who is in danger.
250: Good training pays off in Germany. A degree or a completed [[Ausbildung]], a vocational training, opens the way to better-paid jobs.
251: Since 2000, German law gives children the right to an upbringing without violence. Hitting a child can be punished as bodily harm, even by a parent.
252: Germany only allows monogamy: a person can be married to one partner at a time. Marrying again while still married, bigamy, is a crime.
253: Within two weeks of moving, residents must register their new address at the [[Einwohnermeldeamt]], in many cities called the [[Bürgeramt]].
254: Courts want to see that a marriage has truly broken down. Living apart for a year, the [[Trennungsjahr]], shows this and leaves time to reconsider.
255: The [[Jugendamt]], the youth welfare office, gives parents advice and support with upbringing. Its family counseling is free of charge.
256: Running a restaurant needs a [[Gaststättenerlaubnis]], a license from the responsible authority, which checks that the owners and premises are suitable.
257: An [[Abendgymnasium]] is a school for working adults. Classes run in the evening, so students can earn the [[Abitur]] while keeping their jobs.
258: The [[Jugendamt]] mainly supports families, but when a child is in danger, for example beaten or starving, it can take the child into care.
259: The career information center of the [[Bundesagentur für Arbeit]] helps people explore jobs and find an apprenticeship, called a [[Lehrstelle]].
260: Germany has compulsory schooling, the [[Schulpflicht]]. Children must attend their lessons, and homeschooling is generally not allowed.
261: It is never too late for the [[Abitur]]. Evening schools, [[Abendgymnasien]], teach adults after work, so they can study without giving up their jobs.
262: Article 3 of the [[Grundgesetz]] says all people are equal before the law, and since 1994 it adds that no one may be disadvantaged because of a disability.
263: From 14, young people can be held criminally responsible. Courts then apply [[Jugendstrafrecht]], juvenile law, which focuses on education.
264: [[Rosenmontag]] is the high point of carnival, with big parades in Cologne, Düsseldorf and Mainz. People dress up in colorful costumes and masks.
265: Only a civil wedding at the [[Standesamt]] is legally valid in Germany. A religious ceremony can follow, but it does not replace the civil one.
266: Night rest, the [[Nachtruhe]], usually runs from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. During this time, neighbors should not be disturbed by noise.
267: Adults decide for themselves where and with whom they live. At 22 the daughter is [[volljährig]], of full age, so the parents must accept it.
268: The theory test for a driving license is offered in many foreign languages, including English, Turkish and Arabic, so it tests the rules, not the German.
269: From age three until school starts, children have a legal right to a [[Kindergartenplatz]]. Going there is still voluntary, not compulsory.
270: The [[Volkshochschule]], or VHS, is an adult education center found in almost every town, with affordable courses in languages, computers and more.
271: Decorating a [[Tannenbaum]], a fir tree, is a German custom that spread around the world. Many families put it up and trim it on Christmas Eve.
272: Germany only recognizes marriage between two people. Being married to two partners at the same time is bigamy, which is a criminal offense.
273: For help with raising children, parents can turn to the [[Jugendamt]]. It offers advice, parenting courses and referrals to family counseling.
274: Opening someone else's mail on purpose breaks the [[Briefgeheimnis]], the secrecy of letters. It is protected by Article 10 of the [[Grundgesetz]].
275: A divorce is decided by the [[Familiengericht]], the family court. At least the partner who files the divorce application must be represented by a lawyer.
276: Rude or unfair treatment by an official can be reported to the head of the agency. This formal complaint is called a [[Dienstaufsichtsbeschwerde]].
277: Turning down an applicant only because they are a mother is discrimination. Germany's equal treatment law, the [[AGG]], forbids this in hiring.
278: Using a wheelchair says nothing about skill with numbers. Rejecting someone only because of a disability is discrimination and is forbidden by law.
279: The [[Hausordnung]] sets rules everyone in the building follows, such as quiet hours, cleaning the stairwell, or where the rubbish bins go.
280: A tax assessment can be challenged with an objection, an [[Einspruch]], sent to the tax office. It usually has to be filed within one month.
281: Refusing entry because of skin color violates the right to [[Gleichbehandlung]], equal treatment. The [[Grundgesetz]] bans disadvantage based on origin.
282: Elections need many helpers. Citizens can be called up as election workers, [[Wahlhelferinnen und Wahlhelfer]], and may refuse only for important reasons.
283: Decisions and bills from authorities can be challenged with a [[Widerspruch]]. The agency then has to review its decision; the deadline is usually one month.
284: When jobs change fast, learning cannot stop after training. Continuing education, [[Weiterbildung]], keeps skills up to date throughout a working life.
285: Value added tax, [[Umsatzsteuer]] or [[Mehrwertsteuer]], is already part of the price of things people buy. It is not deducted from a salary like income tax.
286: The [[Betriebsrat]] is elected by the employees themselves. It represents their interests and has a say in matters such as working hours and dismissals.
287: Employees cannot simply quit from one day to the next. They must respect the notice period, the [[Kündigungsfrist]], and resign in writing.
288: Germany's special responsibility toward Israel comes from the Holocaust, the murder of six million Jews by the Nazi regime.
289: Skin color has nothing to do with serving tables. Rejecting an applicant for it is racial discrimination, banned by the equal treatment law, the [[AGG]].
290: A new product that is broken gives buyers legal rights. They can make a complaint, [[reklamieren]], and ask the seller for a repair or a replacement.
291: Members of certain churches pay [[Kirchensteuer]], which the state collects along with income tax. It is usually eight or nine percent of the income tax.
292: Religious freedom is protected by the [[Grundgesetz]]. Everyone may choose a faith, change it, or have none at all, and others must respect that.
293: Painting eggs, [[Eier bemalen]], is a popular Easter custom. Children often search for hidden eggs that, the story goes, the [[Osterhase]] brought.
294: [[Pfingsten]], or Pentecost, is a Christian feast fifty days after Easter. Its Monday is a public holiday in every German state.
295: For many centuries Christianity shaped Europe's calendar, art and values. Germany's churches, holidays like Christmas and Easter, and many traditions grew from it.
296: Advent means arrival. It covers the four Sundays before Christmas, and many homes light one more candle on the [[Adventskranz]] each Sunday.
297: Starting with a recruitment agreement in 1961, many workers came from Turkey. Today people with Turkish roots are the largest migrant community in Germany.
298: East Germany signed labour agreements with socialist partner countries. So most of its migrants came from Vietnam, Poland and Mozambique as [[Vertragsarbeiter]], contract workers.
299: West Germany needed workers during its economic boom and called them [[Gastarbeiter]], guest workers, because it expected them to return home. Many stayed.
300: In 1955 West Germany signed its first recruitment agreement with Italy. Agreements with Spain, Greece, Turkey and other countries followed later.
301: Baden-Württemberg's shield is gold with three black lions. They recall the old Swabian rulers whose lands became part of the state.
302: The [[Neckar-Odenwald-Kreis]] takes its name from the Neckar river and the Odenwald hills in the north of Baden-Württemberg. The other districts lie in other states.
303: The [[Landtag]] of Baden-Württemberg is elected for five years. Most German states use this term, while the federal [[Bundestag]] is elected for four.
304: In Baden-Württemberg, young people may vote for their town council and district from age 16. They can help decide what happens right where they live.
305: Baden-Württemberg's flag has two horizontal stripes, black on top and gold below. The colours match the black lions on a gold shield in its coat of arms.
306: Each state has a [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]]. It offers neutral information on politics and democracy, free for everyone, without party bias.
307: Stuttgart is the capital of Baden-Württemberg. The state parliament and the state government both sit there, in the heart of the Neckar valley.
308: Baden-Württemberg lies in Germany's southwest corner. It borders France along the Rhine and Switzerland near Lake Constance, with Bavaria to its east.
309: German states are led by a [[Ministerpräsident]], elected by the state parliament. In Baden-Württemberg this person heads the state cabinet in Stuttgart.
310: Foreign policy belongs to the federal level. Only the [[Auswärtiges Amt]] in Berlin speaks for Germany abroad, so no state has its own foreign minister.
311: Bavaria's coat of arms shows the famous blue and white diamond pattern, the [[weiß-blaue Rauten]]. You see the same diamonds on Bavarian flags and signs.
312: Altötting is a district in Upper Bavaria, best known for its pilgrimage chapel. The other names belong to Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia and Schleswig-Holstein.
313: The Bavarian [[Landtag]] is elected every five years. Most German states use this term, which is one year longer than the federal parliament's.
314: Bavaria has not lowered its voting age for local elections. Voters there must be 18 to choose their mayor and town council, unlike in several other states.
315: Bavaria's colours are white and blue. The flag comes either in two stripes or in the well-known diamond pattern, both used officially.
316: Bavaria's [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] gives neutral, non-partisan information on politics. Every German state runs one of these agencies.
317: Munich is Bavaria's capital. The state parliament meets there in the Maximilianeum, a grand building above the river Isar.
318: Bavaria is in the southeast and is Germany's largest state by area. It borders Austria and the Czech Republic and reaches up into the Alps.
319: In Bavaria, as in most states, the head of government is the [[Ministerpräsident]]. The [[Landtag]] elects this person, who then forms the state cabinet.
320: Bavaria has many ministries, but foreign affairs is not among them. Relations with other countries are a federal task handled by the government in Berlin.
321: Berlin's coat of arms shows a black bear on a white shield. The bear has stood for the city for centuries and appears all over Berlin.
322: Pankow is one of Berlin's twelve [[Bezirke]], or boroughs, in the city's north. Altona is in Hamburg, and the other two are regions in other states.
323: Berlin's state parliament is called the [[Abgeordnetenhaus]], the House of Representatives. Its members are elected for five years.
324: Berlin lets people vote from age 16 when electing the assembly of their borough, the [[Bezirksverordnetenversammlung]]. Teenagers can shape their own district.
325: Berlin's flag has red stripes at the top and bottom with a white band in the middle. The black bear from the coat of arms sits on the white.
326: Berlin, like every state, has a [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]]. It provides balanced, free information on politics to everyone who lives there.
327: A city-state is a city that is a federal state on its own. Germany has three of them: Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen. Saarland, Brandenburg and Hessen are larger territorial states.
328: Berlin sits in the northeast of Germany and is completely surrounded by the state of Brandenburg. It is both the capital and a state of its own.
329: Berlin's head of government is the [[Regierender Bürgermeister]], the Governing Mayor. This person leads the [[Senat]], Berlin's state government.
330: In Berlin, ministers are called senators. There is no senator for foreign affairs, because dealing with other countries is the federal government's job.
331: Brandenburg's coat of arms shows a red eagle on a white shield. The eagle is the old symbol of the region and also appears on the state flag.
332: Prignitz is a rural district in the northwest of Brandenburg. Rhein-Sieg is in North Rhine-Westphalia, Vogtland in Saxony, and Amberg-Sulzbach in Bavaria.
333: Brandenburg's [[Landtag]] meets in Potsdam and is elected for five years. Most German state parliaments share this five-year term.
334: Brandenburg lets young people vote in local elections from age 16. It even allows 16-year-olds to vote for the state parliament, which only some states do.
335: Brandenburg's flag is red and white, two horizontal stripes with the red eagle from the coat of arms in the middle.
336: Brandenburg's [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] offers neutral information, publications and events on politics. Every German state has one.
337: Potsdam is Brandenburg's capital, just southwest of Berlin. It is famous for Sanssouci, the palace and park of the Prussian kings.
338: Brandenburg lies in eastern Germany and wraps all the way around Berlin. It borders Poland to the east, along the rivers Oder and Neisse.
339: Brandenburg's government is led by a [[Ministerpräsident]]. The state parliament elects this person, and they appoint the ministers of the cabinet.
340: Brandenburg has ministers for finance, justice and the interior, but none for foreign affairs. Germany's foreign policy is decided only at the federal level.
341: Bremen's coat of arms shows a silver key on a red shield. It is the key of Saint Peter, patron saint of Bremen Cathedral.
342: Hemelingen is a [[Stadtteil]], a city district, in the southeast of Bremen. Altona belongs to Hamburg, Pankow to Berlin, and Babelsberg to Potsdam.
343: Bremen's state parliament, the [[Bürgerschaft]], is elected for four years. Most other German states elect their parliaments for five years.
344: In Bremen, people may vote from age 16 for the [[Bürgerschaft]], the state parliament. So teenagers there have a say in state politics, not only local matters.
345: Bremen's flag has many red and white stripes, often with a checkered edge. Locals call it the [[Speckflagge]], the bacon flag, because of how it looks.
346: In Bremen, the [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] provides neutral, free information on politics and democracy. Every German state has such an agency.
347: Bremen is a city-state, a city that forms a federal state of its own. The state of Bremen includes two cities: Bremen itself and Bremerhaven on the coast.
348: Bremen is the smallest German state. Its two cities, Bremen and Bremerhaven, lie in the northwest and are surrounded by Lower Saxony.
349: Bremen is led by the [[Präsident des Senats]], who is also the city's mayor. The Senate is Bremen's state government, a tradition from its days as a free city.
350: Bremen's senators run areas like finance, justice and the interior. Foreign relations are a federal responsibility, so Bremen has no senator for them.
351: Hamburg's coat of arms shows a white castle with three towers on a red background. The castle and gate recall the old walled city.
352: Altona is one of Hamburg's seven districts, called [[Bezirke]]. It was once an independent city on the Elbe before it became part of Hamburg.
353: Hamburg's state parliament is the [[Bürgerschaft]], the citizens' assembly. Like most German state parliaments, it is elected for a five-year term.
354: In Hamburg, people can vote for the district assemblies, the [[Bezirksversammlungen]], from age 16. Hamburg also lets 16-year-olds vote for its state parliament.
355: Hamburg's flag is red with a white castle, so its colors are white and red. The castle stands for the city and its long history as a free trading city.
356: Each state has its own [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]]. It offers neutral, free information on politics, with no party or church behind it.
357: A city-state, or [[Stadtstaat]], is a single city that is also a federal state. Germany has three of them: Hamburg, Berlin and Bremen.
358: On the map, look for the small city-state in the north, on the Elbe river. Hamburg is surrounded by Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.
359: Hamburg's head of government is the [[Erster Bürgermeister]], the First Mayor. They lead the [[Senat]], which is Hamburg's name for its state government.
360: Foreign policy belongs to the federal government, so no state has a minister for it. Hamburg's senators run state matters like justice, finance and the interior.
361: Hesse's coat of arms shows a lion with red and white stripes on a blue shield. In German it is often called the [[bunter Löwe]], the colorful lion.
362: The Main-Taunus-Kreis lies between Frankfurt and Wiesbaden. A [[Landkreis]] groups several towns and villages together for local administration.
363: The [[Hessischer Landtag]], the state parliament of Hesse, is elected for five years. It meets in Wiesbaden, the state capital.
364: Hesse keeps the voting age for local elections at 18. Some other states allow 16, so the rule depends on which state you live in.
365: Hesse's flag has two stripes, red on top and white below. The same red and white appear on the striped lion in the state's coat of arms.
366: For neutral facts on politics, go to the [[Hessische Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]]. It offers free brochures and events for everyone.
367: Frankfurt is the biggest city in Hesse, but the capital is Wiesbaden. The state government and the [[Landtag]] are both based there.
368: Hesse lies near the center of Germany, with Frankfurt and the river Main in its south. On the map, look for the state in the middle, west of Thuringia.
369: In thirteen of the sixteen states, the head of government is the [[Ministerpräsident]]. Only the three city-states use mayor titles instead.
370: Germany's relations with other countries are a federal task, handled by the [[Auswärtiges Amt]] in Berlin. So Hesse has no foreign minister of its own.
371: The coat of arms shows a black bull's head for Mecklenburg and a red griffin for Pomerania, the two historic regions that form the state.
372: The [[Mecklenburgische Seenplatte]], the Mecklenburg Lake District, has hundreds of lakes. It includes the Müritz, the largest lake entirely inside Germany.
373: The state parliament of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, its [[Landtag]], is elected for five years. That is the most common term among the German states.
374: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern lets people vote in local elections from age 16. So young people can help elect their town council and their district council, the [[Kreistag]].
375: The flag combines the blue and white of Pomerania with the yellow and red of Mecklenburg. Four colors for one state made of two historic regions.
376: The [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern informs people about politics. Its job is to stay neutral and not favor any party.
377: Rostock is the biggest city, but the capital is Schwerin. The state parliament even meets in Schwerin Castle, the [[Schweriner Schloss]], on an island in a lake.
378: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is in the far northeast, along the Baltic Sea coast. It borders Poland and includes the islands of Rügen and Usedom.
379: As in most German states, the government is led by the [[Ministerpräsident]]. The [[Landtag]] elects this person, who then appoints the state ministers.
380: Under the Basic Law, the [[Grundgesetz]], relations with foreign states are a federal matter. That is why Mecklenburg-Vorpommern has no foreign minister.
381: Lower Saxony's coat of arms shows a white horse leaping on a red shield. It is called the [[Sachsenross]], the Saxon horse, an old symbol of the region.
382: Ammerland is a rural district in the northwest of Lower Saxony, near Oldenburg. It is known for its tree nurseries and rhododendron gardens.
383: The [[Niedersächsischer Landtag]] in Hannover is elected for five years. Its members pass state laws and elect the state's head of government.
384: Lower Saxony was one of the first states to let 16-year-olds vote in local elections. Young people can help choose their town and district councils.
385: Lower Saxony's flag uses the national colors black, red and gold. What makes it different is the state coat of arms in the middle, with the white horse.
386: The [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] in Lower Saxony gives neutral information on politics and democracy, open and free to everyone.
387: Hannover is the capital of Lower Saxony. The [[Landtag]] meets in the [[Leineschloss]], a former royal palace in the city center.
388: Lower Saxony is the large state in the northwest, on the North Sea coast. It is so big that it completely surrounds the city-state of Bremen.
389: Lower Saxony is led by the [[Ministerpräsident]], the minister-president. The title means the person who presides over the state cabinet of ministers.
390: States in Germany handle things like police, schools and courts, but not foreign policy. That stays with the federal government, so there is no foreign minister.
391: North Rhine-Westphalia's coat of arms has three parts: the river Rhine, the white horse of Westphalia, and the rose of Lippe, the regions that formed the state.
392: The Rhein-Sieg-Kreis surrounds the city of Bonn and is named after the rivers Rhine and Sieg. Its seat is the town of Siegburg.
393: North Rhine-Westphalia's state parliament, the [[Landtag]], is elected for five years. It meets in Düsseldorf, on the banks of the Rhine.
394: In North Rhine-Westphalia, the voting age for local elections is 16. So teenagers can help choose their mayor and city council, the [[Stadtrat]].
395: The flag of North Rhine-Westphalia is green, white and red. Green stands for the Rhineland, and white and red come from the colors of Westphalia.
396: Each state has a [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]]. In North Rhine-Westphalia it offers free, neutral material about politics and democracy.
397: Cologne is the largest city in North Rhine-Westphalia, but the capital is Düsseldorf. The state government and the [[Landtag]] sit there.
398: North Rhine-Westphalia lies in the west, bordering the Netherlands and Belgium. It has more people than any other German state, around the Rhine and the Ruhr.
399: The head of government in North Rhine-Westphalia is the [[Ministerpräsident]]. The [[Landtag]] elects them, and they lead the state cabinet.
400: Foreign policy is decided at the federal level, so Germany speaks with one voice abroad. That is why North Rhine-Westphalia has no foreign minister.
401: The coat of arms joins three old symbols: the cross of Trier, the wheel of Mainz and the lion of the Palatinate, topped by a crown of vine leaves.
402: The Westerwaldkreis lies in the Westerwald hills in the north of Rhineland-Palatinate. The area is known for its blue and grey stoneware pottery.
403: Rhineland-Palatinate elects its state parliament, the [[Landtag]], for five years. It meets in Mainz, in a historic building known as the [[Deutschhaus]].
404: Rhineland-Palatinate keeps 18 as the voting age for local elections. The rule differs between states, because each state sets its own local election law.
405: Rhineland-Palatinate's flag has the national colors black, red and gold. Its coat of arms sits in the upper left corner, the part closest to the flagpole.
406: In Rhineland-Palatinate, the [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] offers free, neutral information to help people understand politics.
407: Mainz is the capital of Rhineland-Palatinate, on the Rhine. It is also the city of Johannes Gutenberg, who developed printing with movable type.
408: Rhineland-Palatinate lies in the southwest, bordering France, Luxembourg and Belgium. The Rhine and the Moselle flow through its many wine regions.
409: Rhineland-Palatinate is led by the [[Ministerpräsident]]. The title is shared by most German states; only Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen use mayor titles.
410: Foreign policy belongs to the federal level, so Rhineland-Palatinate has ministers for justice, finance and the interior, but no foreign minister of its own.
411: Saarland's coat of arms is split into four fields. Each one recalls a historic territory that once ruled parts of the region before it became a state.
412: Saarland is small and has only six districts, and [[Neunkirchen]] is one of them. The other options lie in Mecklenburg, Bavaria and North Rhine-Westphalia.
413: Voters in Saarland choose their state parliament, the [[Landtag]], every five years. That is the same term used by almost every German state today.
414: Each state sets its own voting age for local elections. Saarland has kept it at 18, while several other states let people vote locally from 16.
415: Saarland's flag shows black, red and gold, just like the national flag, with the state coat of arms placed in the middle to tell them apart.
416: The [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] offers neutral information about politics. It does not favour any party and is open to everyone in Saarland.
417: Saarbrücken is both the capital and the largest city of Saarland. Its name comes from the river Saar, which flows right through the city centre.
418: Saarland sits in the far southwest of Germany. It borders France and Luxembourg, and its only German neighbour is Rhineland-Palatinate.
419: Saarland's government is led by the [[Ministerpräsident]], who is elected by the state parliament, much like the Chancellor is elected at federal level.
420: States in Germany run schools, police and justice, but foreign relations stay with the federal government. So Saarland has no foreign minister.
421: Saxony's coat of arms has black and gold stripes crossed by a green band of leaves, called the [[Rautenkranz]]. It is a symbol that goes back centuries.
422: The [[Vogtlandkreis]] lies in the southwest of Saxony, near Bavaria, Thuringia and the Czech border. The other districts belong to different states.
423: The Saxon [[Landtag]] is elected for five years at a time. Between elections, it passes state laws and keeps an eye on the state government.
424: In Saxony, people can vote in municipal and district elections once they turn 18. Some other states lower this to 16, so the rule depends on the state.
425: Saxony's flag is simply white over green. These two colours have stood for Saxony for a long time and are easy to spot on official buildings there.
426: For neutral facts about politics in Saxony, the place to go is the [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]]. It publishes free material and runs events.
427: Dresden on the river Elbe is the capital of Saxony. Leipzig is actually the larger city, which is why many people pick the wrong one on the test.
428: Saxony lies in the east of Germany. It is easy to find on a map because it borders both Poland and the Czech Republic.
429: In Saxony, as in most German states, the head of government is the [[Ministerpräsident]]. The parliament elects this person, and they choose the ministers.
430: Justice, finance and the interior are state matters, so Saxony has those ministers. Foreign affairs are a federal task, so there is no Saxon foreign minister.
431: The coat of arms of Saxony-Anhalt joins the Saxon black and gold stripes with the bear of Anhalt, reflecting the two historic names in the state's title.
432: The [[Börde]] district is named after the fertile plain around Magdeburg. Its rich soil makes it one of the best farming areas in Germany.
433: The [[Landtag]] of Saxony-Anhalt sits for a five-year term. When it ends, voters elect a new parliament, which then chooses the next state government.
434: Saxony-Anhalt lets people vote in local elections from age 16. Local decisions on schools, parks and transport affect young people too.
435: The flag of Saxony-Anhalt has a yellow stripe above a black one. On official flags, the state coat of arms sits in the centre.
436: In Saxony-Anhalt, the [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] explains politics without taking sides. Every German state has a similar office.
437: Magdeburg on the river Elbe is the capital, home to the state parliament and government. Halle, Dessau and Wittenberg are important cities in the same state.
438: Saxony-Anhalt lies in the middle of eastern Germany, surrounded by Lower Saxony, Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia. It has no border with another country.
439: Saxony-Anhalt is led by a [[Ministerpräsident]]. Titles like Prime Minister or Mayor are used elsewhere; Mayor is for the head of a town.
440: Germany speaks to other countries through the federal government. That is why Saxony-Anhalt, like every state, has no foreign minister of its own.
441: Schleswig-Holstein's coat of arms joins two historic regions: two blue lions stand for Schleswig, and a white nettle leaf on red stands for Holstein.
442: [[Nordfriesland]] lies on the North Sea coast and includes islands such as Sylt. It is part of Schleswig-Holstein, Germany's northernmost state.
443: Every five years, people in Schleswig-Holstein elect a new state parliament, the [[Landtag]], which meets in the capital, Kiel.
444: In Schleswig-Holstein, voting in local elections starts at 16. Several states have made this choice, though federal elections follow their own rules.
445: Schleswig-Holstein's flag has three stripes: blue, white and red. The colours come from the state's coat of arms and its historic regions.
446: Schleswig-Holstein does things a little differently: political education is run by the [[Landesbeauftragte für politische Bildung]], a state commissioner.
447: Kiel is the capital, not Lübeck or Flensburg. It lies on the Baltic Sea and hosts a large sailing festival every summer, the [[Kieler Woche]].
448: Schleswig-Holstein is at the very top of the map. It is the only German state with coasts on both the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, and it borders Denmark.
449: The head of government in Schleswig-Holstein is the [[Ministerpräsident]]. Elected by the state parliament, they lead the state cabinet in Kiel.
450: A state like Schleswig-Holstein needs ministers for justice, money and internal affairs. Relations with other countries are handled in Berlin instead.
451: Thuringia's coat of arms shows a lion with red and white stripes on a blue shield, surrounded by small stars. Look for the striped lion on the test.
452: The [[Wartburgkreis]] is named after Wartburg Castle near Eisenach, where Martin Luther translated the New Testament into German.
453: Thuringia elects its state parliament, the [[Landtag]], for five years. It meets in Erfurt and elects the state's head of government.
454: From age 16, people in Thuringia can vote for their local council and mayor. States decide this themselves, so the age differs across Germany.
455: Thuringia's flag is white over red. These are the colours of the striped lion in the state's coat of arms, which helps you remember them.
456: In Thuringia, the [[Landeszentrale für politische Bildung]] is the place for neutral information on politics. Its brochures and events are open to all.
457: Erfurt is the capital and the largest city of Thuringia. It is known for the [[Krämerbrücke]], an old bridge lined with houses and small shops.
458: Thuringia lies right in the centre of Germany and is covered in forests and hills. That is why it is often called the [[grünes Herz Deutschlands]].
459: Thuringia's government is led by the [[Ministerpräsident]]. The title is used in nearly every German state; only city-states use other names.
460: Foreign affairs are a federal task under the Basic Law, so Thuringia has a justice, finance and interior minister, but never a foreign minister.
